name: Tea tree extract

lead: Tea tree extract and oil come from an Australian shrub and are common in acne and blemish products for their antibacterial reputation.
A Cochrane review summarised on Wikipedia found one low-quality acne trial favouring the oil. Trials specific to the extract were not found.

paras: The oil's main component is terpinen-4-ol, which has antimicrobial activity in lab tests.
Skin irritation and allergy occur, especially with oxidised oil. Swallowing is highly toxic, and a possible link to breast enlargement has been reported.

lead: Tea tree extract and tea tree oil derive from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia, a plant native to eastern Australia. The oil is promoted for acne, dandruff and minor skin infections, and tea tree extract appears in cleansers and blemish products.[1]

The published evidence is mostly for the oil rather than extracts. A 2015 Cochrane review, as summarised on Wikipedia, found one low-quality trial showing benefit for acne lesions. Wikipedia also reports skin irritation and allergy, toxicity if swallowed, and a possible link to breast enlargement in boys and men.[1]

paras: ISO 4730 defines tea tree oil by terpinen-4-ol at about 35 to 48 percent, with gamma-terpinene and alpha-terpinene; the oil changes chemically on air exposure.[1] Commercial production began in the 1920s after chemist Arthur Penfold reported antiseptic properties, with large plantations established in the 1970s and 1980s.[1] A Korean cosmetic patent lists tea tree extract among soothing ingredients in a skin formulation.[2]
Researchers have studied tea tree extract as a corrosion inhibitor for steel and as an antioxidant and antibacterial load in nanofibre membranes.[3][4] These do not concern skin appearance.

Small registered trials of tea tree oil include a 2012 pilot gel study for facial acne (18 participants) and several trials of eyelid treatments for blepharitis and demodex mites.[5][6][7] Wikipedia, citing a 2015 Cochrane review, says evidence for acne is limited to one low-quality trial.[1] No clinical trial of tea tree extract (as distinct from oil) for skin was found.

Wikipedia reports that ingestion of the oil is highly toxic, with poisonings in Australia mostly among children, that skin use can cause irritation and allergy more often when the oil has oxidised, that a 2018 NIEHS study identified four constituents as endocrine disruptors, and that dogs and cats have been harmed by high-dose topical use. It is not an approved drug in the US but is used in skin care, and Australia approves it as a complementary medicine for aromatherapy.[1]

timeline.event: Commercial tea tree oil production begins after Arthur Penfold's antiseptic findings.[1]
